newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Retail king seen unlikely to win Creditanstalt.
newsitem.headline: Retail king seen unlikely to win Creditanstalt.

text.p: Karl Wlaschek, a one-time bar pianist who netted 15 billion schillings ($1.37 billion) from the sale of his retail empire in July, on Monday emerged as a surprise bidder for Creditanstalt, but his chances of success appeared slim.

The 79-year-old king of the nation's supermarket scene added an unexpected twist to the country's longest-running privatisation project, rivalling bids by heavyweights Bank Austria and a long-standing group led by insurer EA-Generali.
EA-Generali had to struggle to come up with an offer for all of the state's 19.9 million voting shares in the bank.

Socialist-controlled Bank Austria's bid for Creditanstalt, firmly in the conservative camp, kicked up a political storm in Austria where political and economic might are carefully divided along political lines..

But whether Wlaschek could steal their colourful show and emerge as the white knight in the politically-fraught battle for the one-time banker to the Austro-Hungarian emperors was more than doubtful, analysts said.

"Wlaschek? I've never even heard of him. I don't really think this is very serious," a London-based analyst told Reuters on the condition of anonymity. "He's probably going to be ruled out anyway because of his credentials."
Wlaschek, well-known in Austrian society circles but notoriously reclusive when it comes to business affairs, was not available for comment.

The frail, white-haired entrepreneur became one of Austria's richest men when, in a surprise coup, he sold his Billa supermarket chain to Germany's Rewe group in July. Billa is the country's biggest employer, with sales of some 50 billion schillings last year.

After his abrupt abdication from the retail throne, Wlaschek was some 15 billion schillings richer and was widely expected to retire after 45 years in business. Now, analysts said, he added what amounted to an interesting sidebar in the seemingly endless Creditanstalt saga.

"Obviously it will be down to the value of the bids to a certain extent but I would have thought the government was unlikely to sell to a private individual," said Victoria Maxwell, Austria analyst at James Capel in London.
In a tightly-worded statement on Monday, Finance Minister Klima listed the three bids but declined to reveal any details.
The EA-Generali consortium said it aimed to take control of 74 percent of the government's 19.9 million Creditanstalt ordinary voting stock.

Union Bank of Switzerland, Commerzbank, Belgium's Bacob, Banca Commerciale and savings bank Die Erste joined EA-Generali and are expected to take on the remaining 26 percent of the state's stake to place it on the market later.
Bank Austria has offered to buy the entire stake for some 16 billion schillings in cash, but analysts have voiced doubts about the bank's ability to come up with the financing.
"We will now carefully evaluate all the bids in order to find the best possible solution," Klima said, adding he expected to make a final decision on the winning bid before year-end.
